ro82fm.text: Coinbase says it blocked $4.7 million in cryptocurrency transfers to scammers promoting a fake giveaway using an AI-generated deepfake of Elon Musk during a Tesla livestream that attracted more than 500,000 viewers. The deepfake took place during Tesla's "flying car" demonstration, when scammers created a fake YouTube livestream that appeared to broadcast the event. The fraudulent stream featured an AI-generated video of Musk, cryptocurrency wallet addresses, and a QR code, promising viewers that any cryptocurrency they sent would be doubled. According to Coinbase, hundreds of its customers attempted to send millions of dollars to the scammers over about two hours, including many longtime users of the exchange. However, the company says its AI-powered fraud-prevention systems detected the scam and blocked about 91% of the attempted transfers, totaling $4.7 million. Unlike traditional cryptocurrency theft involving compromised accounts or stolen credentials, victims in this campaign voluntarily made the crypto transfer after believing the livestream was real. Coinbase explained that this makes scams like these difficult to detect because the transactions are created and approved by legitimate account holders. "Most fraud defenses are built to spot activity the customer didn't authorize," Coinbase explained. "That's not what happened here. The customer was logged in, the customer pressed confirm, and the customer believed it was the opportunity of a lifetime." AI agents intervene to stop transfers Coinbase says its scam prevention system uses machine learning models to analyze outgoing cryptocurrency transfers in real time, identifying suspicious activity associated with giveaway scams, brand impersonation, and newly created wallet addresses. When a suspicious transfer is detected, an AI agent engages the customer in a short conversation, explaining the characteristics of the suspected scam and asking questions intended to help them recognize the fraud. The system also assigns confidence scores to the agent's responses before presenting them to customers, allowing it to determine when additional safeguards may be necessary. Coinbase says its AI agent had never encountered this particular campaign before but recognized the underlying scam techniques, including promises to multiply cryptocurrency, time pressure tied to a live event, and irreversible transfers. The company claims the entire detection and intervention process operated automatically, without human involvement. "What's notable is that the agent had never seen this scam. Deepfake giveaways tied to a live product launch weren't in its training," Coinbase said. BleepingComputer contacted Coinbase to ask how many transfers reached the scammers and how much cryptocurrency was stolen, but has not yet received a response. Elon Musk and his companies have long been popular lures for cryptocurrency scams, with fraudsters hijacking verified Twitter accounts, sending fake giveaway invitations via email, and flooding TikTok with fraudulent promotions. Scammers have also used deepfake videos of Musk to promote fraudulent cryptocurrency investment platforms, while a separate campaign involving compromised verified Twitter accounts stole more than $580,000 in cryptocurrency in just one week. To avoid falling victim to these types of scam campaigns, users should independently verify cryptocurrency promotions through official websites and social media accounts rather than trusting livestreams or QR codes displayed in videos. 1hmm8uy.text: A New York federal bankruptcy judge on Tuesday greenlit the sale of Spirit Airlines’ employees’ data to Google, a decision that follows the tech giant’s agreement to abide by restrictions on how it uses and deidentifies the information. After shutting down in May, Spirit announced it would sell Google its former employees’ data for $10 million, prompting a lawsuit from the flight attendants’ union and criticism from 121 federal lawmakers. Soon after the outcry began, Google agreed to new terms designed to better protect sensitive data. On November 9, the union withdrew its objection to the sale, citing Google’s pledge to exclude employees’ health and medical data, alcohol and drug testing results, safety and disciplinary records and identification documents. The tech giant also agreed to what the union called a “rigorous de-identification process” and a mandatory review of the deidentified data by an independent assessor chosen in collaboration with the union. Google also agreed not to attempt to reidentify the data. In signing off on the sale, U.S. Bankruptcy Judge Sean Lane said the “procedures for the deidentification, transformation and preparation of the data” comply with applicable data protection laws, according to a court filing. Google did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The company has said it intends to use the data for AI model training. The agreement is the first of this scale to emerge in the AI era. The dataset includes an estimated 100 million emails and half-billion Microsoft Teams messages, which experts say will be useful for training agents handling professional tasks. While the flight attendants’ union has celebrated the protections it won, Arjun Bhatnagar, the CEO of the consumer privacy startup Cloaked, said the data sale still poses a threat to employees. “Google said it won't try to reidentify anyone, and that promise is supposed to follow the data, but every time a dataset like this gets copied, licensed or breached, someone always finds an opening to connect all the data points,” he said via email. No previous articleNo new articlesSuzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1cqo8ol.text: Senior Trump administration officials on Wednesday insisted that recent service outages underpinning much of everyday life — and U.S. national security — are not the result of a coordinated digital attack on the country. Over the last week, a global blackout of common Microsoft products, a nationwide ground stop by the FAA, glitches in the banking system and National Security Agency, the country’s largest spy agency, have rattled the public and policymakers on both sides of the aisle who fear the high-profile disruptions are secretly the work of foreign adversaries. “With the processes that we put in place, what we have seen over the last ten days is not an orchestrated attack by a foreign malign actor,” Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton testified before the House Homeland Security Committee. “We do not have any indication that it would be.” Throughout the panel’s annual worldwide threats hearing, Clayton, along with Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia, sought to address bipartisan concerns, chalking up the interruptions to emerging AI capabilities, aging infrastructure, and increased system patching and upgrades. Despite the bureau’s cyber teams being involved in the various investigations “from day one,” agents have found no evidence that malicious cyber activity caused the recent failures, according to Raia. “At this point, there is no indication whatsoever that there is any cyber malicious activity related to any of those incidents.” He later added that the FBI would continue to work with DHS and ODNI “to be to be 120 percent sure.” Different tone The administration’s past efforts to assuage the public, especially around the four-hour-long groundstop, have been undercut by Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Mullin himself. Each has offered varying explanations for the extraordinary action, including when the DHS chief went on television and said that, based on conversation with unnamed tech executives, AI may have been responsible. Mullin struck a different note before Congress. “I'm 98 percent confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our system.” Mullin added that the administration would hold a phone call with representatives from the private sector about informing their customers when an upgrade is coming so they can adequately prepare. “We're not pressuring the industry to do it. We just want to have a conversation and say maybe we should start communicating because what happens online is a tremendous amount of fear,” he said. “I think all of us can understand it but there's no cause for it.” Clayton, who on Tuesday explained the outage of an internal NSA network was the result of maintenance related PHP, went the furthest of the trio in offering possible reasons for the rush of technical failures. “We are in an environment where the rate of patching, the rate of upgrading of systems, is increasing,” he told the panel. “That is the result of advancements in compute and in applications, we should expect that as people are patching, and as people are upgrading systems.” He noted malicious actors are using such advances to augment their capabilities, including scanning to identify vulnerabilities in systems. “We need to use the increased compute and the increased capabilities to combat that scanning,” Clayton said. “That has been going on inside a number of our sophisticated financial institutions and others. So we are meeting this threat but it's something that we need to continue to do.” The spy chief later urged the American people to “understand that we are in the process of upgrading our systems.” “I'm looking around this room and I'm seeing different systems from many different decades. Some of them are actually a combination of decades,” he said. When you have combinations of old and new equipment on a particular network, that makes upgrades and things like this challenging. We're going to go through this challenge but I think we're going to come out the other side stronger than any country in the world.” No previous articleNo new articlesMartin Matishakis the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

1flzb7u.text: A reported cyberattack on Wellington IT has exposed sensitive information belonging to members of 50 credit unions, the majority of which are located in Ireland. Wellington IT is a Belfast-based supplier whose services are used by about 50 credit unions, including 43 in Ireland. While the company has not publicly disclosed a security incident, Minister of State Robert Troy confirmed to RTÉ that Wellington IT is the third-party service provider linked to the cybersecurity incident involving credit unions, resulting in the exposure of data from about 40 credit unions in Ireland. The company reportedly notified affected organizations of a data breach that posed a risk of financial fraud, impersonation, and targeted phishing to their members. According to the Irish Examiner, which saw the notices, Wellington IT informed customers that an automated script made five million requests to exploit an authorization flaw in the company's infrastructure. The attack unfolded between October 2 and 4, 2026, and the attacker accessed private records using valid credentials. However, the firm said it lacked activity logs that would specify which member data was compromised and therefore cannot verify the impact on individual payees. Minister R. Troy characterized the massive delay in Wellington IT notifying the credit unions as "not acceptable." At this time, the total number of impacted individuals is unknown. Sensitive information exposed At least six credit unions have independently disclosed impact linked to the incident, including Capital Credit Union, Phoenix Credit Union, St. Canice's Credit Union, First South Credit Union, Malahide Credit Union, and Limerick & District Credit Union. The announcements confirmed unauthorized access to payee information, with some noting that members' login credentials and funds haven't been affected, while others are working to determine exactly what was exposed. The notices list the following payee records saved in online banking platforms as potentially exposed: Payee name or name associated with the payee's bank account Nickname the member used to save the payee, if provided International Bank Account Number (IBAN) Bank Identifier Code (BIC) Bank account number Bank sort code Payee address information Payment reference information entered for the saved payee The records could also reveal which credit union member saved a particular payee. Account passwords, PINs, payment card details, and online banking credentials were unaffected, but union members are advised to remain vigilant for phishing and impersonation attempts. BleepingComputer has contacted Wellington IT to learn more about the incident, and we will update this post with their response once we receive it. 1g2xd4o.text: Two leading members of the Senate urged the White House on Tuesday to launch a national effort to more robustly confront AI-enabled cyber threats in light of recent security incidents involving artificial intelligence. In a letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, Sens. Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.) and Mike Rounds (R-S.D.) warned that AI is “rapidly increasing the ability to discover and exploit weaknesses in software” and that the country’s defenses “are not keeping pace.” “The fundamental problem is that AI can discover software weaknesses and help attackers exploit them faster than many organizations can respond,” the senators said. “Even when fixes are available, testing and installing patches across interconnected systems can take weeks or months, potentially disrupting essential services.” The letter cites recent incidents where AI was used to discover obscure bugs and power cyber intrusions in Japan. The senators also raised concerns from banks about AI agents, which are increasingly accessing bank accounts. Several U.S. banks have said they are unable to tell whether AI agents are rogue or are accessing data on behalf of customers. Chinese-developed AI models are also being used widely for a variety of nefarious purposes, the lawmakers said. Rounds is the chairman of the Senate Armed Services subcommittee on cybersecurity and has repeatedly called on the White House to do more to confront risks posed by AI. The senators said the White House task force on AI, which Clayton chairs, needs to speed up the development and deployment of defensive AI-powered tools while also establishing security standards for autonomous AI agents. They called on the task force to convene a meeting with AI developers, cybersecurity companies, critical infrastructure operators, the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST), the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and other agencies. The defense tools should be able to “continuously identify vulnerabilities, develop and test fixes and and block attacks before they spread,” they wrote, and CISA should be in charge of accelerating the adoption of the tools across banks, hospitals, utilities and government agencies. “The United States has the technological expertise to lead this effort,” they said. “What is missing is a coordinated national strategy to bring these capabilities together, establish common security standards, and put effective defenses into widespread use.” Clayton was also urged to start a “national cyber defense grand challenge” that can show how AI defenses can “cut the time from discovery of a critical vulnerability to effective protection.” The letter comes days after the FBI released an urgent warning about a Chinese tool able to automate significant parts of the cyber intrusion process. The system was used in dozens of real-world attacks in Japan, South Korea and the U.S. A newly released Government Accountability Office investigation conducted in the spring also found that the four most-used AI platforms — ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, and Grok — all provided terrorist attack plans in a real-world test to determine AI safety risks. Clayton has not commented on the letter but has spoken publicly in recent days about the need to use AI to discover and patch vulnerabilities. He said a recent spate of technology outages impacting major banks, tech companies and airlines are tied to efforts to patch vulnerabilities discovered at a faster pace than ever before by defenders using AI scanners. “Lots of institutions, because these vulnerabilities have been identified, are patching. They’re taking their systems down, they’re upgrading them, they’re putting patches in place… This is being done on a much larger scale because everybody recognizes it’s time to upgrade their systems,” Clayton told Fox Business on Tuesday. “And as they upgrade them, they’re not coming back as expected in all cases. And in some cases, systems have to hand off to other systems, and those handoffs are not coming back as expected. But this is just an upgrade in patching, an upgrade in systems.” No previous articleNo new articlesJonathan Greigis a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.Suzanne Smalley is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

1v7l5x8.text: A flaw in NGINX's HTTP/2 support can allow an attacker to run code on servers with HTTP/2 enabled, without needing to log in. The decade-old flaw, CVE-2026-123007, dubbed "nginx2root," has been present in NGINX's open-source code since version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. Fixed versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 came out today. F5, the company behind NGINX, says attackers can run code where ASLR is turned off or can be bypassed. Security researchers at Wiz said they bypassed ASLR and ran code through the flaw in tests. Xint's researchers said they ran code through it with nothing more than a reachable HTTP/2 port. Code run this way gets the permissions of an NGINX worker process. Getting root on the host takes a second way to raise privileges, according to CIRCL, the Computer Incident Response Center Luxembourg. In Xint's tests, code running as a worker could get root on the host through a separate bug in the Linux kernel's SCTP code, even when NGINX ran inside a Docker container. Neither the vendor nor the Wiz and Rapid7 researchers have reported any attacks exploiting the flaw so far. CISA's Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog did not list it as of today. Proof-of-concept code for the flaw is publicly available on GitHub, but its notes state it is suitable only for demonstrating the attack against a freshly started Docker container on the same machine. Every open-source release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8 is vulnerable, according to NGINX's security advisories. That includes 1.31.8 from October 21, as well as the October 14 security releases 1.31.7 and 1.30.6. Wiz PoC NGINX Plus is affected too, in 37.x releases before the fixed builds and in R34 to R36, according to the vendor advisory. Today's releases also fix four more flaws that the vendor says can lead to code execution under the same ASLR condition. It scores all five 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0. Each flaw can be reached only in a particular setup: Flaw What it needs CVE-2026-123007 HTTP/2 turned on CVE-2026-123633 HTTP/2, with requests passed to a backend server while the worker is running low on worker_connections CVE-2026-123634 A proxied server name built from variables, plus a server-side include (SSI) or mirror subrequest to a location that looks up the same name CVE-2026-121810 HTTP/3 turned on CVE-2026-113425 NGINX used as a mail proxy HTTP/2 is on where a listen directive includes http2, or where http2 on is set. Running openssl s_client with -alpn h2 against a server shows whether it accepts HTTP/2: the output reads ALPN protocol: h2 if it does. Behind a CDN, test the NGINX origin itself, because an origin that accepts only HTTP/1.1 cannot be attacked through HTTP/2. Fixes, Workarounds and Signs of Attack These releases fix CVE-2026-123007, according to F5: NGINX Open Source 1.31.0 to 1.31.8 (mainline): fixed in 1.31.9 NGINX Open Source 1.9.5 to 1.30.6, including older branches such as 1.28: fixed in 1.30.7 NGINX Plus 37.1.0 to 37.2.0.1: fixed in 37.3.0.1 NGINX Plus 37.0.0 to 37.0.7.1: fixed in 37.0.8.1 NGINX Plus R34 to R36: no fix listed Versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 fix all five flaws, according to NGINX's release notes. On NGINX Plus, 37.3.0.1 and 37.0.8.1 fix four of the flaws, and the CVE-2026-123633 fix was introduced in the earlier builds 37.2.0.1 and 37.0.7.1. After upgrading, restart NGINX fully or use its live binary upgrade. A reload alone leaves the old executable running, and existing connections can stay on old worker processes. The official Docker images for NGINX had 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 tags as of today, including Alpine variants. Ubuntu and Debian had not shipped fixed packages as of today. Ubuntu's CVE status page listed nginx as vulnerable on its releases from 16.04 to 26.10, and Debian's security tracker listed it as vulnerable in bookworm, trixie, forky and sid. A distribution package can carry a fix without changing the version number that nginx -v reports, so compare the full package version with the distribution's own advisory. Xint PoC The vendor lists workarounds for only two of the five flaws. For the resolver flaw, CVE-2026-123634, avoid SSI and mirror directives, and do not build a proxied server name from variables. For the mail proxy flaw, CVE-2026-113425, limit listeners to trusted networks. CIRCL's response guidance lists turning off HTTP/2 as a temporary mitigation until you can upgrade. That blocks CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633, but not the other three flaws. Turning off HTTP/3 where it is used removes the setup that CVE-2026-121810 needs. On NGINX 1.25.1 and later, set http2 off; in each affected server block and remove http2 from its listen directives. On 1.9.5 through 1.25.0, remove http2 from the listen directive, so listen 443 ssl http2; becomes listen 443 ssl;. Then restart NGINX where needed and rerun the openssl check to confirm the server no longer accepts HTTP/2. Until the Linux kernel's SCTP bug is fixed, the same guidance advises that hosts not using SCTP, a network transport protocol like TCP, block its kernel module from loading. One way is to add the line install sctp /bin/false to a .conf file in /etc/modprobe.d/. That does not unload a module already loaded or turn off SCTP built into the kernel. For signs of an attack, CIRCL suggests looking for NGINX workers that start unexpected programs, workers that exit abnormally or leave core dumps, long-lived HTTP/2 connections with heavy incoming traffic but few logged requests, and unusual outbound connections or DNS lookups. A clean access log does not rule out an attack, because HTTP/2 control frames do not normally show up there as requests. None of these signs is proof on its own. Rapid7's version of the attack needs about 128 GB of HTTP/2 traffic, according to its technical analysis. The attack took two and a half minutes in its demonstration. On links slower than about 300 Mbit/s, the transfer would run past NGINX's default one-hour connection limit, and the attack would fail. The method also depends on a glibc memory-copy routine that is chosen on x86-64 CPUs with the avx512f and avx512vl features. Wiz ran its tests on official NGINX 1.31.7 and 1.31.8 builds, using HTTP/2 over TLS on 64-bit systems, according to its disclosure post. Xint's attack worked against its test servers on AWS, GCP and Azure, including over a public IP address, according to its research report.

1ta6vep.text: Swati KhandelwalNov 18, 2026Network Security / Vulnerability Six critical vulnerabilities in F5 BIG-IP allow an attacker to crash the Traffic Management Microkernel (TMM) without logging in, disrupting traffic until the TMM restarts. Each flaw needs a specific setup on a virtual server: an iRule that uses a particular command, or an APM policy that includes two particular kinds of agent. F5, which makes BIG-IP, disclosed the flaws today and says they may also allow remote code execution. The company has released engineering hotfixes and lists no workaround. The company rates all six 9.8 under CVSS v3.1 and 9.3 under CVSS v4.0. They are stack-based buffer overflows in BIG-IP's data plane, the part that processes almost all of its network traffic. The management side is not exposed, according to the company. None of the company's advisories says the flaws have been exploited. WatchTowr researcher Sina Kheirkhah reported four, and the company found the other two itself. Five of the flaws are in iRules, a BIG-IP feature that administrators use to manage traffic, and one is in BIG-IP's APM module. Some also affect BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and BIG-IP CNF, part of the company's BIG-IP Cloud-Native Edition. Each flaw needs the setup listed below on a virtual server: CVE-2026-123637: an APM per-request policy that includes both the Client Information agent and Endpoint Security agents. Affects BIG-IP APM only. CVE-2026-121805: an iRule that uses PEM::subscriber on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP PEM, BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. CVE-2026-120292: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses MR::message route. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. CVE-2026-120285: an HTTP profile and an iRule that uses PSC::ip_address. Affects BIG-IP (all modules), BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes and, as of today, BIG-IP CNF. CVE-2026-116953: an iRule that uses GENERICMESSAGE::route on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP (all modules) and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. CVE-2026-120722: an iRule that uses DNS::scrape on client traffic. Affects BIG-IP DNS and BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes. The company's advisory lists BIG-IP CNF as not vulnerable, but its CVE record, updated today, lists CNF as affected. F5's security notification lists the 22 advisories it published today, including 10 for NGINX. For the six critical flaws, the only fixes are engineering hotfixes, builds that the company issues between its normal software releases. No scheduled release is listed as a fix, and the advisories provide no workaround until a hotfix is installed. The company warns that "engineering hotfixes do not undergo the extensive QA assessment of scheduled software releases." Its hotfix policy adds that they come with no warranty or promise that they will work. A system on a custom engineering hotfix needs a new one from the company's support team. BIG-IP Next for Kubernetes is fixed in BNK-2.4.2-EHF1, BNK-2.3.4-EHF1 and BNK-2.2.5-EHF1, for versions 2.4.0 to 2.4.2, 2.3.0 to 2.3.4 and 2.2.0 to 2.2.5. BIG-IP CNF, on the same version ranges, is fixed in CNF-2.4.2-EHF1, CNF-2.3.4-EHF1 and CNF-2.2.5-EHF1 for CVE-2026-121805 and CVE-2026-120285. The company checks only versions that are still within technical support, so an older release missing from its tables has not been shown to be safe. Today's flaws differ from CVE-2026-94127, an APM flaw that F5 disclosed on September 22 and that was later exploited. The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added it to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the same day. That flaw is a heap-based buffer overflow in APM setups that serve as OAuth authorization servers, allowing attackers to run code without logging in. Today's six are stack-based overflows that need different settings. Six Other BIG-IP and BIG-IQ Flaws Today's advisories also cover six lower-rated flaws in BIG-IP and BIG-IQ, each with its own fix. The scores below are CVSS v3.1: CVE-2026-125274 (iControl SOAP, 8.8): A user with network access and at least the Guest role can send an unauthorized management request. The company says this may allow them to run system commands, create or delete files, or disable services. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10 and 17.1.3.6, and in BIG-IQ 8.4.2.3. Until then, the SOAP advisory explains how to limit iControl SOAP access to trusted networks and warns that blocking it on self-IP addresses may break high-availability setups. CVE-2026-120718 (iControl REST, 8.1): iControl REST tokens may not expire as expected. An attacker who already holds a token may be able to extend how long it stays valid unless its owner deletes it. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.2, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6. As a workaround, scripts that create tokens can be changed to delete them when they are no longer needed. CVE-2026-125272 (APM, 7.5): When an APM access profile on a virtual server has a per-request policy with a form-based Logon Page, an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes as the six critical flaws. CVE-2026-126822 (APM SAML, 7.5): When an access profile is set up as a SAML Service Provider (SP), an attacker can crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes. Until then, the company suggests removing the SAML Auth agent if SAML SP is not needed, and limiting access to that virtual server to trusted client networks. CVE-2026-126336 (APM SAML, 7.5): A SAML SP agent with encrypted assertions turned on lets an attacker crash TMM without logging in. It is fixed in BIG-IP 21.1.0.3, 17.5.1.10, and 17.1.3.6, and the company recommends a high-availability setup to reduce the impact. CVE-2026-121812 (APM and SSL Orchestrator, 7.5): A per-request policy with the tmm.access.policytrace database key turned on lets an attacker crash TMM. The key is off by default. APM is fixed in the same engineering hotfixes, and for SSL Orchestrator the advisory lists fixes on the 21.1 and 17.1 branches only.

rhcn9h.text: Ravie LakshmananNov 18, 2026Vulnerability / Cyber Attack A critical security flaw in Apache Roller, an open-source, Java-based blogging platform, has come under active exploitation in the wild, according to the Apache Software Foundation (ASF) The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-129448 (CVSS score: 9.8), is a case of unauthenticated deserialization in the XML-RPC endpoint that could lead to remote code execution. "Deserialization of Untrusted Data in Apache Roller versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 allows an unauthenticated remote attacker to execute arbitrary code," project maintainers said. "The XML-RPC endpoint accepts vendor extension types and deserializes them before authenticating the requester." ASF also noted that the vulnerability is the same as CVE-2026-82384 (CVSS score: 9.8), which was patched in September 2026 and listed only Apache Roller 6.1.5 as affected. "This issue is being actively exploited," it added. ASF did not share any details on how the vulnerability is being exploited, or who is being targeted as part of these efforts. A security researcher named n0mi1k has been credited with finding the flaw, and Matt Raible has been acknowledged for reporting it. Users are advised to upgrade to Apache Roller 6.1.6 or later, which disables the extension types and rejects XML-RPC requests when the XML-RPC feature is disabled. If immediate patching is not an option, it's recommended to set "enabledForExtensions" to "false" in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the "/roller-services/xmlrpc" servlet mapping, and then restart Roller. "Disabling XML-RPC in the administration UI is not enough, because older versions deserialize the request before checking that setting," ASF noted.

6d6ahq.text: Hackers compromised Microsoft's official Agent Framework Python package on PyPI, publishing two malicious versions designed to steal cloud credentials and other sensitive information from developers' systems. Microsoft Agent Framework is Microsoft's open-source toolkit for building AI agents and coordinating them in workflows. It's a fairly popular tool with roughly 200,000 monthly downloads on PyPI. The malicious releases, versions 1.26.1 and 1.26.2, were published on November 17, 2026, and contained a credential stealer that executed automatically during normal Python startup in affected environments, even when the Agent Framework package was not imported. Both versions retained their dependency on the legitimate agent-framework-core 1.26.0 package, allowing the framework to function normally while the malware ran in the background. Multiple security firms discovered and documented the attack, including Socket, Step Security, and Ox Security. Attack overview Source: Ox Security Version 1.26.1 contained a credential stealer that harvested secrets from environment variables, local configuration files, and other running processes where permissions allowed, targeting Azure, AWS, GitHub, Docker, Hugging Face, OpenAI, and other services. The malware also attempted to obtain Azure managed identity access tokens and Azure DevOps OIDC tokens, potentially giving attackers access to additional cloud resources. Version 1.26.2 added GitHub Actions OIDC token requests and searches of GitHub runner directories. According to Socket and StepSecurity, the first malicious release used agent_framework_meta.pth to execute the credential stealer in agent_framework_meta/_telemetry.py during Python startup. The second release restored the original package initializer and moved the malicious code into af_runtime_diag.pth and af_runtime_diag.py. Both versions exfiltrated collected data to the same attacker-controlled endpoint, https://webhook[.]site/d381fd80-ec62-42ad-8f5c-d1b15103c9bb. Collecting data from breached environments Source: Ox Security PyPI quarantined the first malicious release, but the attacker published a second version roughly 2.5 minutes later, which was also quarantined about eight minutes afterward. The second release indicates that the attacker still had publishing access after the initial quarantine. It remains unclear how the attacker gained access to publish malicious releases under Microsoft's official PyPI project. BleepingComputer has contacted Microsoft to learn what the point of breach was, but we have not received a response by publication time. Developers who installed either malicious version should isolate affected environments, avoid running Python or pip until they are secured, and rebuild from a known-clean environment using the safe 1.26.0 release. Any potentially exposed credentials that were within the reach of the compromised environment should be rotated immediately. To determine the exact level of compromise, investigators should look for the specific webhook URL path in egress logs and distinguish blocked requests from completed transfers. 19evh0.text: Disruptions at the National Security Agency entered their second day on Wednesday as the spy organization worked to get its internal communications network back up and fully running. The system, known as NSA Net, experienced intermittent outages on Tuesday, leading the agency to tell its work force to stagger arrivals at its headquarters at Fort Meade, Maryland. It eventually closed its campus to most employees by the evening, according to sources. Non-essential personnel were sent a "Code Gray" notification late Tuesday night, informing them to arrive at 10 a.m. Wednesday. However, that time has already been moved to the afternoon and could change again, said a source familiar with the ongoing situation. Meanwhile, the agency’s cafeteria, and a Starbucks located on its campus, remain closed. The same person said the network is working but NSA leaders are still staggering personnel because the login process is the most taxing process on the system. They also said comments made Tuesday by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton — that the outage was due to maintenance affecting PHP, a common programming language — were correct. It remains unknown if the vulnerability was AI-derived or human-driven. The source speculated that it might take another day or two for full restoration of the classified network, but insisted that the spy agency’s classified national security work remains unimpeded. The NSA did not immediately respond to a request for comment. The outage is the latest in a series of high-profile technical disruptions in the last week, including a global outage of Microsoft products, a nationwide flight stoppage and problems with bank services. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-NY) on Wednesday called on President Donald Trump and Clayton to “form a dedicated red team of trained intelligence professionals to challenge the assumption that these outages are just business as usual.” Schumer, who is lobbying his colleagues to become Majority Leader following the outcome of the midterm elections, said it is “too coincidental that all these outages happened within a few days for us to think it's business as usual. We have to get to the bottom of this.” He urged the administration to form the team and report its findings to Congress by December 1. Testifying on Wednesday before the House Homeland Security Committee, Clayton said he understands that the “timing of these incidents can raise questions and it should.” “The American people should ask us these questions, but, based on what we know today, after a great deal of diligence, these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes,” he added. “They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.” No previous articleNo new articlesMartin Matishakis the senior cybersecurity reporter for The Record. Prior to joining Recorded Future News in 2021, he spent more than five years at Politico, where he covered digital and national security developments across Capitol Hill, the Pentagon and the U.S. intelligence community. He previously was a reporter at The Hill, National Journal Group and Inside Washington Publishers.

iaf0k8.text: Russian state-backed hackers are using information stolen from cloud accounts to impersonate trusted contacts and launch new espionage attacks against people in their victims' professional networks, according to new research. The hacking group, known as Cold Relic or ColdRiver, has previously targeted government officials, defense contractors and nonprofit organizations across Europe and North America. U.S. authorities have linked the group to Russia's Federal Security Service (FSB). In a report published Wednesday, Google's cybersecurity unit Mandiant described how the hackers used data stolen from one U.S. organization in late 2025 to help compromise a second entity. During the first attack, the hackers took control of an administrator account and used it to download the organization's entire cloud drive and employee directories. They also searched for emails, passwords and personnel records, apparently looking for information they could use in future operations. The hackers remained inside the organization's systems for several months. They continued reading emails through third-party applications and found ways to regain access after the organization changed passwords and reset user sessions. Even after losing access to the network, the hackers continued targeting the organization and its contacts by sending emails that appeared to come from employees. In a separate attack this year, Cold Relic used information stolen in the earlier breach to pose as an employee and approach someone at another U.S. organization through an encrypted messaging app. The hackers first struck up a conversation with the target before sending malicious links designed to steal Microsoft account login details and authentication tokens. To make the messages appear more convincing, the links led to documents related to their conversation, making the phishing attempt harder to spot. The hackers ultimately gained access to an account at the second organization and downloaded large amounts of data from the user's cloud storage, Google said. The researchers did not identify either U.S. organization or disclose what information was stolen. Google said Cold Relic frequently uses compromised websites to redirect targets to phishing pages, concealing the actual destination and allowing the attackers to assess visitors before displaying malicious content. The approach reflects Cold Relic's broader strategy of exploiting relationships between victims. Rather than relying solely on phishing emails, the hackers use stolen correspondence, employee information and familiar identities to make subsequent attacks more convincing, according to the report. Google has tracked the group since 2015 and observed evidence of new phishing operations as recently as this month. Although Cold Relic has attracted less public attention than some other Russian state-backed hacking groups, Google said it has maintained a steady pace of operations. No previous articleNo new articlesDaryna Antoniukis a reporter for Recorded Future News based in Ukraine. She writes about cybersecurity startups, cyberattacks in Eastern Europe and the state of the cyberwar between Ukraine and Russia. She previously was a tech reporter for Forbes Ukraine. Her work has also been published at Sifted, The Kyiv Independent and The Kyiv Post.

17id278.text: In 2024, an employee at engineering firm Arup was tricked into transferring $25 million after attending a fake video conference featuring deepfake versions of their colleagues. A year later, Marks & Spencer (M&S) suffered a major cyberattack after attackers used social engineering to gain access through a third-party helpdesk. More recently, attackers have impersonated IT support staff to convince employees to hand over remote access to their devices. While the tactics differ, these incidents raise an important question for IT and security teams: how can organizations be confident that someone requesting access or authorizing a sensitive action is who they claim to be? We examine these attacks and explore how stronger identity verification and more secure workflows can help organizations defend against similar threats. The Arup Deepfake Fraud A finance employee at engineering firm Arup's Hong Kong office received an email in January 2024 that appeared to come from the company's UK-based CFO, requesting a series of transactions. Initially suspicious, the employee was convinced the request was genuine after joining a video conference featuring what appeared to be the CFO and several colleagues. However, the meeting was a deepfake. According to Hong Kong police, the attackers had used publicly available video and audio to create a convincing pre-recorded conference. The employee subsequently made multiple transfers, losing approximately HK$200 million (US$25.6 million). The M&S Cyberattack In April 2025, British retailer Marks & Spencer (M&S) suffered a major cyberattack that disrupted operations for weeks. Online orders were suspended, contactless payments and Click & Collect services were affected, and customer data was stolen. M&S initially estimated the incident would reduce its 2025/26 operating profit by around £300 million before mitigation. The attack was linked to the Scattered Spider cybercriminal group, known for using social engineering to gain access to corporate networks. M&S later confirmed that attackers had gained entry by deceiving employees at a third-party contractor, rather than exploiting a technical vulnerability in its systems. Fake IT Support Microsoft recently reported a cyberattack campaign in which threat actors impersonated IT support staff through Microsoft Teams, tricking employees into handing over remote access to their devices. The attackers contacted employees through external Teams messages or calls, posing as internal IT personnel. Using convincing pretexts such as urgent technical issues, they persuaded employees to grant remote control through screen sharing or legitimate support tools like Quick Assist. Once connected, the attackers used PowerShell to install malicious software, establish persistent access and gather information about the compromised network. Microsoft also observed attempts to move laterally towards critical infrastructure, including domain controllers and certificate authorities. The Common Thread: Trust Replacing Verification Impersonation Exploits Familiar Trust Signals Social engineering has long been a key technique in attackers’ arsenals. They don't need sophisticated malware or technical exploits to compromise an organization if they can convince someone that they're a trusted colleague. Deepfake technology makes this particularly concerning, as familiar faces and voices can be recreated. But even without AI, attackers can use convincing pretexts and trusted communication platforms to make fraudulent requests appear legitimate. Trusted Processes Can Become Attack Vectors Password resets and remote IT support are routine activities, but they can also give attackers opportunities to gain access if requests aren't properly verified. Third-party providers expand the potential attack surface; organizations may have strong controls over their own systems but less visibility into how external support teams verify identities and authorize sensitive actions. Employees Can't Be Expected to Spot Every Impersonation Attempt Security awareness training helps employees recognize suspicious requests, but even well-trained staff can be deceived by convincing impersonation attempts. Attackers will carry out reconnaissance beforehand to gather information that makes their social engineering attempts appear like routine requests. Organizations need reliable verification processes that support employees when they're asked to make security-sensitive decisions, rather than leaving them to judge whether someone can be trusted. How Can Organizations Mitigate These Risks? Strengthen Identity Verification at the Service Desk Rather than relying on security questions or personal information that attackers may have obtained, service desk teams should use trusted authentication methods to confirm callers' identities. Specops Secure Service Desk helps organizations build this verification into their service desk processes. Agents can verify callers using more than 15 MFA factors, including options that don't require a phone, with integrations for existing identity platforms such as Duo and Okta. This helps ensure that sensitive account recovery actions are supported by reliable identity checks, reducing opportunities for attackers to exploit service desk procedures. To see it in action, explore our interactive walkthrough and discover how agents can securely verify callers before carrying out sensitive account actions. Build Verification Into Business Workflows As organizations introduce self-service portals, internal chatbots and automated IT processes, it's important that these systems follow the same verification standards as traditional support channels. A password reset request made through an internal chatbot, for example, should still require strong identity verification before the request is processed. It’s here that solutions like the Specops Authentication API can help, by allowing organizations to add secure workforce authentication and identity verification to their existing applications, automated processes and business workflows. By integrating verification directly into these processes, organizations can apply consistent security checks at critical points without relying entirely on manual intervention. Independently Verify Sensitive Requests For financial transactions, privileged access, and other sensitive requests, organizations should require independent confirmation through trusted channels. This might include contacting the requester using previously verified details or introducing additional authentication into approval workflows. Verify IT Support Requests Before Granting Access Where support processes are managed through internal applications or automated workflows, additional identity verification can help ensure that sensitive requests are made by authorized users. These measures should be supported by broader security controls like phishing-resistant MFA and least-privilege access, while monitoring for suspicious account activity. Make Strong Verification Part of Everyday Security As social engineering tactics become more convincing, organizations can't rely on employees recognizing every fraudulent request. Strong identity verification, independent approval processes and clear security procedures can help reduce the risks. By building these checks into service desks, applications and everyday workflows, organizations make it harder for attackers to turn a convincing impersonation into a successful compromise.
